## How Do LLMs Work? Transformers Explained (2026)
Large language models work by predicting the next token in a sequence, trained on trillions of examples of human text. A token is a word or sub-word unit — the word "understanding" might be split into "under" + "stand" + "ing." The model sees a sequence of tokens, computes probability distributions over its entire vocabulary (typically 100,000-200,000 tokens), and selects the most likely continuation. This process repeats, one token at a time, until the response is complete. [...] That last row matters more than it looks. At the very end of the network, only the last vector in the sequence is multiplied by the unembedding matrix to produce the next-token distribution. Every other vector in the final layer is "wasted" at inference time — but during training, every position predicts its own next token in parallel, which is what makes the math tractable on trillion-token corpora. ### Embedd

The target sequence is used by the loss function. It is not supplied to the transformer as a separate answer. The transformer receives the input sequence, and a causal attention mask prevents each position from reading later input positions. When the model predicts (t\_3) from the position containing (t\_2), its representation can depend on (t\_0), (t\_1), and (t\_2), but it cannot use (t\_3). ## Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback(RLHF)-ChatGPT
After the reward model has been trained, the next step is to use reinforcement learning (RL) to optimize the original language model with respect to the reward model. At this point in the RLHF system, we have an initial LM that can generate text and a preference model that assigns a score to the text based on how well humans perceive it. RL is used to fine-tune the original LM to improve its performance and generate text that is more in line with human preferences. plan.title: How ChatGPT Works: Predicting One Token at a Time
plan.description: Large language models like ChatGPT work by predicting the next token, learned from trillions of examples of human text. This video explains tokens, attention, training, and how human feedback turns a text predictor into an assistant.

beats.narration: ChatGPT does not know how its sentence will end. It has no plan. It only ever answers one question: what comes next?

props.text: It only ever answers one question: what comes next?

beats.speaker: narrator

beats.narration: First, text is chopped into tokens. A token is a word or a piece of a word. The word understanding might become under, stand, and ing.
beats.speaker: narrator

beats.narration: Each token becomes a list of numbers called an embedding. Since attention cannot see order by itself, position information is added too.
beats.speaker: narrator

beats.narration: Picture a researcher at a computer, reading through mountains of text. The model does something similar, but with trillions of examples of human writing.

props.alt: person typing at a desk with screens

beats.speaker: narrator

beats.narration: Next comes attention. Each token looks at the tokens before it, and gathers context. This repeats through many blocks, stacked one on top of another.
beats.speaker: narrator

beats.narration: At the end, the model scores every token in its vocabulary, typically 100,000 to 200,000 of them. Each gets a probability of being next.

props.label: tokens scored for every single prediction

beats.speaker: narrator

beats.narration: Then one token is picked, using settings like temperature. It is added to the prompt, and the whole loop runs again. Predict, append, repeat.
beats.speaker: narrator

beats.narration: So how does it learn? In training, it reads real text and guesses the next token. Then it measures the error, and nudges its numbers to do better.
beats.speaker: narrator

beats.narration: Billions of repeats teach it grammar, word meanings, facts, and long-range connections. The result is a base model: a powerful text predictor, but not yet a helpful assistant.
beats.speaker: narrator

beats.narration: To make it helpful, OpenAI used human feedback. People wrote example answers, and the model was fine-tuned to imitate them.

props.clip_query: people working at laptops in office
clip_queries: people working at laptops in office

beats.speaker: narrator

beats.narration: Then labelers ranked different answers from best to worst. Those rankings trained a reward model, which learned to score answers the way people would.
beats.speaker: narrator

beats.narration: Reinforcement learning then tunes the model toward higher scores. The effect is striking: a small 1.3 billion parameter InstructGPT was preferred over the 175 billion parameter GPT-3.
beats.speaker: narrator

beats.narration: Even humans disagree. Labelers agreed on rankings only about 73 percent of the time. So the model learns a blurry average of human taste.

props.label: About 73% of rankings matched between labelers
props.title: Labeler agreement

beats.speaker: narrator

beats.narration: So a chatbot is a next-token predictor, trained on huge text, then shaped by people. Remember this: it writes by predicting, one token at a time.

props.text: It writes by predicting, one token at a time.

beats.speaker: narrator

accuracy.reason: Mostly matches the notes, but "Each token looks at the tokens before it" is only true of decoder-only models and is oversimplified. The claim of "trillions of examples" is loosely framed, and "ChatGPT ... has no plan" is stated flatly. The InstructGPT comparison is correct (1.3B preferred over 175B GPT-3).

coverage.reason: Covers tokens, embeddings, attention, the generation loop, pretraining and RLHF. Hallucinations, which the reviewer's note requires, are absent entirely. Attention gets only one thin sentence and there is no explanation of Q/K/V or of why attention helps.

structure.reason: Clear chapters run tokens, transformer, training, then RLHF, and the ending returns to the opening idea. Pacing is steady. Beat 4 interrupts the flow and sits oddly between embeddings and attention.

hook_ending.reason: The opener "ChatGPT does not know how its sentence will end" has some tension. The ending is a restatement ("Remember this: it writes by predicting") rather than a fresh image or new thought.

tone.reason: Plain, accessible and beginner-friendly with short sentences. A little dry, and terms like "reward model" and "embedding" get only light analogies.

visuals.reason: Scene types vary well (diagram, steps, sequence, scale_compare, pictogram). Weak spots: the stock clip of a "researcher at computer" for "mountains of text" is generic, and the stat "100,000+" is fine but the scale_compare bars (1.3 vs 175) are a fair use of real numbers. The pictogram of 73% is acceptable.

originality.reason: The 73% labeler agreement and the 1.3B vs 175B comparison are concrete, but the explanation otherwise uses no memorable analogy and follows a standard tutorial path.

instructions.reason: Length is on target and the language is English. It misses the hallucinations point from the expected content and uses little analogy-based explanation.

language.reason: Fluent and grammatical. Beat 4 ("The model does something similar") is vague, and the "blurry average of human taste" line is a slight overreach.

defects.quote: So a chatbot is a next-token predictor, trained on huge text, then shaped by people.
defects.issue: Never addresses hallucinations or why a next-token predictor invents false facts, which is a core expected point.

defects.quote: Each token looks at the tokens before it, and gathers context.
defects.issue: Oversimplifies attention. It omits how relevance is weighted and implies only a backward-looking mechanism without explaining the causal mask.

defects.quote: Picture a researcher at a computer, reading through mountains of text.
defects.issue: The filler stock-clip beat interrupts the tokens-to-attention flow and the analogy is vague and unhelpful.

defects.quote: So the model learns a blurry average of human taste.
defects.issue: This is an inference not in the notes. The 73% agreement is presented as the cause, while the reward model actually learns from rankings.
A generic stock clip does not illustrate trillions of text examples, so it adds little.

defects.quote: Reinforcement learning then tunes the model toward higher scores.
defects.issue: The RL step is glossed over, and the phrase "OpenAI used human feedback" skips the later-era nuance, with no mention of how current models differ.

missing: Limits: no real understanding or knowledge cutoff
wrong_facts: "Each token looks at the tokens before it" holds only for decoder-only models like GPT; simplified but not wrong for ChatGPT.
judge.summary: A clear, accurate, well-ordered explainer that covers the pipeline from tokens to RLHF with a couple of nice concrete facts. It omits hallucinations, treats attention thinly, and ends on a restatement rather than a fresh image.
